# Serialize manual tenant-repo sync with the periodic scheduler

## Context

The cloud tenant-repo lane exposes two entry paths over the same mirrors and `tenant-repo-sync-revisions.json` state:

- the long-running orchestrator's periodic `TenantRepoSyncService` invocation;
- the operator CLI `node ./ai/scripts/maintenance/syncTenantRepos.mjs`, including the scoped full-replay mode added by `#15748`.

The CLI is documented as the recovery/bootstrap path, but it does not participate in the daemon process's task-state guard.

Live latest-open sweep: checked the latest 20 open issues at `2026-07-23T15:11:38Z`; no equivalent found. The recent all-state A2A claim sweep found no overlapping lane. Semantic and exact-history sweeps surfaced the original scheduler, heavy-maintenance lease, and manual CLI tickets, but no cross-process serialization contract for these two invocations of the same lane.

## The Problem

`syncTenantRepos.mjs` creates an in-memory TaskStateService. `TenantRepoSyncService.runTask()` checks only the injected service's `running` state. The live orchestrator and a separately launched CLI therefore cannot see each other's active tenant-repo sync.

Each process then:

1. reads the whole revisions JSON document;
2. mutates its in-memory copy while processing selected/all repos;
3. writes the whole document back.

A manual replay can race a periodic sweep and produce last-writer-wins loss:

- the CLI may erase a periodic update for another repo;
- the periodic sweep may erase the CLI's successful replay checkpoint;
- failure/backoff increments may disappear;
- a crash during a non-atomic whole-file write may leave unreadable state.

The existing in-process per-repo semaphore controls work inside one invocation. It does not provide cross-process exclusion or atomic manifest commit.

## The Architectural Reality

- This is same-lane serialization, not a request to merge `tenant-repo-sync` with the separate local-only `kbSync` lane.
- The revision manifest is one deployment-wide whole-document state file. Until it becomes a transactional per-repo store, the simplest correctness boundary is one cross-process tenant-repo-sync writer at a time.
- Existing heavy-maintenance lease primitives provide stale-owner/token/recovery precedent, but tenant-repo sync needs a dedicated lease identity so it does not accidentally serialize unrelated maintenance beyond the required correctness boundary.
- The periodic scheduler should defer cleanly when an operator replay owns the lease; that is not an ingestion failure and must not increment repo failure/backoff.
- The CLI needs a bounded held/busy outcome and deterministic exit code rather than silently racing or waiting forever.
- The lease and manifest live under the orchestrator state owner and therefore depend on durable cloud state wiring (`#15759`) for recreate continuity.

Structure-map ownership: existing orchestrator lease primitives, `TenantRepoSyncService`, the manual maintenance script, tenant-repo error taxonomy, and existing unit/integration suites. Reuse sibling primitives; no new subsystem or directory is required.

## The Fix

1. Add one dedicated cross-process tenant-repo-sync lease acquired by every periodic and manual invocation before reading mirrors/revision state or starting repo work.
2. Reuse the existing tokenized stale-owner/recovery discipline where applicable; do not implement a boolean lock with permanent-dead-owner failure.
3. Define bounded contention behavior:
   - periodic invocation: deferred/skipped with a stable non-failure reason and no repo backoff mutation;
   - manual CLI: bounded wait or immediate busy result with stable code and documented exit code.
4. Hold the lease through the final revision-manifest commit and release it in all normal/error paths.
5. Write `tenant-repo-sync-revisions.json` atomically (temporary sibling file + fsync/rename or equivalent proven primitive) so a process crash cannot expose a partially written JSON document.
6. Surface only bounded lease owner class/timestamps/reason codes in diagnostics; never expose PIDs, host paths, repo identities, or command lines publicly.
7. Add a real cross-process or deterministic two-writer witness proving no lost update between periodic and CLI paths.

## Decision Record impact

Aligned with ADR 0014's orchestrator-owned tenant-repo lane and existing heavy-maintenance lease precedent. No ADR amendment: this closes a same-lane concurrency defect without coupling tenant-repo sync to local `kbSync`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Periodic and manual tenant-repo sync acquire the same dedicated cross-process lease before reading or mutating revision state.
- [ ] Two processes cannot concurrently perform repo work or write `tenant-repo-sync-revisions.json`.
- [ ] A held lease makes the periodic invocation defer/skip with a stable non-failure reason and does not change any repo's `consecutiveFailures`, `lastRunAttemptAt`, or checkpoint.
- [ ] A held lease gives the manual CLI a bounded wait or immediate busy result with stable code, deterministic exit code, and updated help text.
- [ ] Lease release occurs on success, returned error-bearing ingestion, thrown error, and process-normal shutdown paths.
- [ ] Stale/crashed lease owners recover safely; a stale lease cannot block the lane forever, and token mismatch cannot release a new owner's lease.
- [ ] Revision-manifest writes are atomic; injected failure before replacement leaves the previous complete JSON readable.
- [ ] A deterministic two-writer or real child-process test proves that disjoint repo updates cannot overwrite each other between manual and periodic paths.
- [ ] Full replay retains `#15752` fail-closed semantics while serialized: old checkpoint remains until an error-free replay commits.
- [ ] Public diagnostics expose only bounded contention/recovery status and timestamps; no PID, host path, repo identity, command line, credential, or raw error leaks.
- [ ] The lock is dedicated to tenant-repo sync and does not couple the lane to local-only `kbSync` or unrelated maintenance work.

## Out of Scope

- Replacing the JSON manifest with SQLite or a distributed database.
- Serializing tenant-repo sync against unrelated `kbSync`, Dream, backup, or defrag lanes.
- Adding a remote replay MCP actuator.
- Changing per-repo in-process concurrency limits.
- Solving deployment state persistence itself (`#15759`).

## Avoided Traps

- Do not rely on in-memory task state for cross-process exclusion.
- Do not reuse the global heavy-maintenance lease if that over-serializes unrelated work; reuse its primitive semantics with a dedicated lease identity.
- Do not treat operator ownership as an ingestion failure or advance backoff.
- Do not release a lease by deleting a path without token ownership validation.
- Do not add a lease while leaving whole-file writes crash-partial.

* test(orchestrator): the backoff term must keep growing across successive crashes (#16551)

Covers the N>1 half of the growth AC, which the first spec did not reach: a fold
that re-derived its base from committed state would read the same number every
restart, because a crash loop never commits. Asserting only the first crash would
have let a flat 2x pass as exponential.

Writing it surfaced a real weakness in the sibling spec. The configured
`backoffCapMs` is 2h, and 1 failure against a 60min base also resolves to 2h — so
the original `nextDueAt` assertion passed whether the multiplier worked or the
value merely hit the ceiling. Both specs now run with `backoffCapMs: 0` (the pure
function's own no-cap default), which is what makes them measure the multiplier
rather than the ceiling.

The cap itself is existing `isRepoDue` behaviour with its own coverage; nothing
here changes it.

* fix(orchestrator): recovery input and in-flight state are different objects (#16551)

Found by @neo-gpt in review. The fold cleared the sidecar on disk but kept the same
object as the live in-flight map, so the first repo to enter protected work rewrote
the whole file from it and re-armed an already-consumed attempt. The next sweep
folded it again, and the next — a recovery that re-arms itself inflates
`consecutiveFailures` without bound on a lane that is succeeding.

The live map is now a fresh object. Recovery INPUT and in-flight STATE have
different lifetimes and one object cannot be both.

Sidecar writes are also lease-fenced now: a whole-file write of this sweep's view
must not clobber a successor that already owns forward progress. The failure is
swallowed rather than propagated, because losing a sidecar write costs one
unrecorded attempt while throwing from the per-repo `finally` would mask the real
error the repo failed with.

The two-repo witness is the smallest one that works. Two repos both RUNNING does
not reproduce it — the residue-holder's own fresh attempt overwrites its stale
entry under the same key and the map empties correctly. The residue-holder must be
suppressed while a SIBLING runs, which the fold itself produces.

A lease-takeover witness was written and REMOVED: it passed against the unfixed
source, so it proved nothing. The lease fence above is reasoned, not witnessed, and
is flagged as such in the review response rather than presented as covered.

* test(orchestrator): witness the lease fence an evicted run must respect (#16551)

The RA2 witness I owed. My own first attempt took the lease over inside
`gitMirror.fetch` and PASSED against the unfixed source, so it proved nothing and
was deleted rather than shipped green.

Ordering is what makes the race reachable: the takeover must land AFTER the
predecessor has persisted its own in-flight record, or its `finally` has nothing to
write and the stale whole-file write never happens. `envelopeEntered` resolves at
the top of the envelope builder, before the gate is awaited, so awaiting it proves
the record already exists. The successor lease and sidecar are written together
inside the lifecycle guard so a renewal tick cannot interleave.

Verified both directions rather than assumed:

  830ac7a378 (pre-fix)  RED  — ENOENT on revisions.json.in-flight: the evicted
                              predecessor's stale finally DELETED the successor's file
  HEAD       (fixed)    GREEN — leaseGuard rejects the stale whole-file write

Asserts exact equality rather than existence: a rewritten-but-present file would
pass a pathExists check while having lost the successor's attempt.

Entry point contributed by @neo-gpt, who could not execute it under a 0% usage gate.

* fix(orchestrator): the in-flight record carries its owner, so a clear is conditional (#16551)

Found by @neo-gpt on the exact production path. `await leaseGuard()` followed by a
write is check-then-act: the lease can expire and a successor legitimately acquire
in the window between the two syscalls, and the resumed predecessor's whole-file
write then DELETES the successor's record. His observation was
`sidecarExists=false; contents=null`.

Fencing the write harder cannot fix this. The check and the write are separate
operations, so any lock narrows the window instead of closing it. The previous
witness only covered takeover BEFORE the check, where the guard still says no.

So the record carries the id of the run that wrote it, and every mutation re-reads
inside the critical section and merges: entries owned by another run are carried
forward untouched, and only our own keys are written or removed. The last writer no
longer wins by virtue of being last — it wins only on keys it owns.

The witness takes over under the SAME repo label, which is the hard case: a
per-label read-modify-write would still clobber it, so only ownership survives.
Verified both directions rather than assumed — RED at b89ef0bafc with
`Received: null` (the file deleted), GREEN here.

* fix(orchestrator): the lease lifecycle guard spans the whole sidecar transaction (#16551)

Fourth finding from @neo-gpt, and the framing was the part I had wrong. Ownership
on the record made the clear conditional, but the read and the write were still two
syscalls with nothing spanning them ACROSS PROCESSES — the previous revision moved
the window from check->write to read->write rather than closing it. A lock that
does not span both cannot close a check-then-act.

`syncTenantRepos` did not receive the lease path, so it is threaded through from
`runTask`. The critical section now holds the lease's OWN lifecycle guard across
ownership re-inspection, read, merge and write.

Reusing the lease guard rather than giving the sidecar its own is his call and it
is right: a sidecar-only mutex serializes sidecar writers while lease ACQUISITION
still interleaves, so it cannot establish generation authority. `runId` stays as
defence-in-depth for the residual that guard's own contract admits — a holder
stalled past `guardStaleAfterMs` resuming inside the verify-to-syscall gap.

The witness asserts the guard REFUSING, not a pending promise. `enterLifecycleGuard`
is bounded (100 attempts x 10ms), so past that budget a contended recovery resolves
`{status: 'held', guardContended: true}`. An assertion written for "still pending"
would fail against CORRECT code on a slow run; the bounded refusal is deterministic
and the stronger claim. Only the recovery path contends at all — acquiring a vacant
name is a plain exclusive create outside the guard — hence the short
`leaseStaleAfterMs` so the successor takes the guarded path.

* fix(orchestrator): the guard fails CLOSED, verifies before writing, and covers the fold (#16551)

Three residuals from @neo-gpt's bounded closure, all real and all confirmed in my
own source before fixing:

1. FAIL-OPEN on contention. `enterLifecycleGuard` returns null once its bounded
   retry budget is exhausted, and the previous revision fell through and ran the
   read-merge-write UNGUARDED — precisely the interleaving the guard exists to
   prevent, and exactly when contention proves another actor is live. It now
   returns without mutating. Skipping costs one unrecorded attempt; proceeding
   costs the invariant.

2. NO OWNERSHIP RE-VERIFICATION before the write. The guard's own contract
   requires it: a holder stalled past `guardStaleAfterMs` can be legitimately

and sits immediately before it. Everything prior is staging on a private temp path
and is discardable.

a failure. The successor owns forward progress, this run's state is merely stale,
and the next sweep re-derives it. Recovery declines the sidecar clear when the

* fix(orchestrator): an attempt that never returns is still an attempt (#16551)

Backoff reads `consecutiveFailures` + `lastRunAttemptAt`, and both advanced only
after the work returned. A failure that prevents the work from returning — OOM,
SIGKILL, host sleep, container stop mid-sweep — therefore left no record that
anything was tried, `due` stayed true, and the lane retried at full cadence.

A crash loop is precisely what backoff exists to dampen, and it was the one
failure class where backoff could not engage: the dampening was available only to
failures polite enough to return.

The record cannot live in the revisions manifest. That file is a commit log and
the #15763 commit-point fence is its contract — an evicted writer must abort
without writing, and a renewal failure must leave no manifest at all. An
in-flight attempt is by definition uncommitted, so it lives beside the manifest
in a `.in-flight` sidecar:

- written after the lease fence and before the git phase, so a repo that never
  entered protected work records no attempt
- cleared in the per-repo `finally` that success, caught failure and lease-lost
  abort all already pass through — per-repo rather than sweep-terminal, so a
  crash during repo B cannot fold repo A's completed attempt into a failure
- folded at sweep start, before the due checks, so a crashed attempt dampens the
  very next decision rather than one sweep later

Commit-then-clear on recovery: a crash between the two re-folds the same attempt
and over-counts one failure, which dampens harder. Clearing first would lose it,
which is the defect being fixed.

Both #15763 fence specs pass untouched, and `isRepoDue` is unchanged — it was
always correct given honest inputs.

The `.in-flight` suffix is asserted literally in the spec rather than through a
shared constant: the on-disk name is the contract between a crashed predecessor
and its successor, and a rename both sides agreed on would leave real residue
unreadable while the spec still passed.

Covers the N>1 half of the growth AC, which the first spec did not reach: a fold
that re-derived its base from committed state would read the same number every
restart, because a crash loop never commits. Asserting only the first crash would
have let a flat 2x pass as exponential.

Writing it surfaced a real weakness in the sibling spec. The configured
`backoffCapMs` is 2h, and 1 failure against a 60min base also resolves to 2h — so
the original `nextDueAt` assertion passed whether the multiplier worked or the
value merely hit the ceiling. Both specs now run with `backoffCapMs: 0` (the pure
function's own no-cap default), which is what makes them measure the multiplier
rather than the ceiling.

The cap itself is existing `isRepoDue` behaviour with its own coverage; nothing
here changes it.

the whole file from it and re-armed an already-consumed attempt. The next sweep
folded it again, and the next — a recovery that re-arms itself inflates
`consecutiveFailures` without bound on a lane that is succeeding.

The live map is now a fresh object. Recovery INPUT and in-flight STATE have
different lifetimes and one object cannot be both.

Sidecar writes are also lease-fenced now: a whole-file write of this sweep's view
must not clobber a successor that already owns forward progress. The failure is
swallowed rather than propagated, because losing a sidecar write costs one
unrecorded attempt while throwing from the per-repo `finally` would mask the real
error the repo failed with.

not reproduce it — the residue-holder's own fresh attempt overwrites its stale
entry under the same key and the map empties correctly. The residue-holder must be
suppressed while a SIBLING runs, which the fold itself produces.
